sentences.text: Before Hon'ble Mr. Justice Hitesh Kumar Sarma Advocates for accused-petitioner :
Ms. B Sarma, Advocate.

Advocate for Respondent :
Mr. Rj Barua, Additional Public Prosecutor, Assam.
Date of hearing and Judgment & Order : 28th of January, 2019.
Judgment

& ORDER (oral) This criminal revision petition is filed, under Section 397, read with Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, against the judgment and order dated 17-08-2009, passed by the Page No.# 2/5 learned Additional Sessions Judge (FTC), Tinsukia, in Criminal Appeal No. 26(3) of 2008, upholding the conviction of the petitioner, under Section 16, read with Section 7 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, (hereinafter referred to as 'the PFA Act'), rendered, vide judgment and order, dated 30-06-2008, by the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate,
Tinsukia, in CR No. 31/2007.

The learned trial Court, sentenced the accused-revision Crl.Rev.P./383/2009 on 28 January, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3387268/
1 petitioner to undergo rigirous imprisonment for six months and to pay a fine of Rs.
1000/-, in default to suffer Simple Imprisonment for one month and the learned appellate Court modified the same to Simple imprisonment of 3 months with fine with default clause.
2.
I have heard Ms. B Sarma, learned counsel for the revision petitioner and Mr. RJ Barua, learned Additional Public Prosecutor, Assam.
3. I have perused the materials on record including the judgments passed by learned trial Court as well as the appellate Court.
I have also gone through the evidence on record.
4. The fact of the case is that, on 12-10-2006, the Food Inspector examined, as PW1, inspected the M/S Delight Bakery at Tinsukia.
Suspecting the bread manufactured there to be adulterated, after observing all required formalities, the Food Inspector had taken sample of such bread.

He purchased six breads, weighing 400 grams each, totalling 2400 grams at a total price of Rs. 72/-.
5.

The sample, so collected, were packed in such a manner so as to prevent moisture etc., and forwarded a part of the sample for analysis by Public Analyst, Assam, a part of the sample was sent to the Joint Director and the other part founded to the Court as per procedure.
6.
The Public Analysts, after necessary examination, gave his report, vide Ext. 14.

Thereafter, the PW1, Food Inspector, lodged a complaint with the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Tinsukia, after obtaining necessary sanction from the competent authority, i.e., the Joint Director of Health Services.

7. On receipt of the complaint, the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Tinsukia, after exhausting all required formalities, explained the offence to the petitioner, under Section 16 read with Section 7 of the PFA Act, to which the petitioner pleaded innocence; therefore, the trial commenced.

8. In this case, prosecution examined as many as 2 witnesses, the Food Inspector/the Page No.# 3/5 complainant as well as PW2, the Office Peon of the Office of the Food Inspector, who accompanied PW1 to the M/S Delight Bakery at Tinsukia, at the relevant point of time.

9. After completion of the trial, the trial Court of the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Tinsukia,
convicted and sentenced the accused-revision petitioner under Section 16, read with Section 7 of the PFA Act for violation of the provision of Rule 32(f) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules,
1955, (hereinafter referred to as 'the PFA Rules) and sentenced him as aforesaid.

10. In appeal, the learned Additional Sessions Judge No. 2, (FTC), Tinsukia, partially allowed the appeal by modifying the substantive sentence of rigorous imprisonment of six months to simple imprisonment for three months, retaining the fine as it is with default clause.
11. I have examined the evidence of the witnesses as available in the records of the learned trial Court.

Crl.Rev.P./383/2009 on 28 January, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3387268/
2 12.
Rule 32(f) of the PFA Rules provides that a level should contain the date, month and the year in which the commodity is manufactured, packed or pre-packed.
13. Now, this Court is required to see whether the accused-revision petitioner violated the aforesaid provisions of Rule 32(f) of the PFA Rules.
14. The offence report, filed vide Ext. 15 is a detailed one.
However, it has not been stated in the offence report that in accordance with the relevant rules provided in the PFA Rules, notice in Form-VI was issued upon the offender.
But, the Form-VI which has been exhibited, vide Ext. 1,
during the evidence of PW1/Food Inspector.
The purchasing of the samples for examination by the Public Analysts has to be mandatorily done after complying with the notice in Form-VI.

Ext. 1 is although indicative of the fact that requirement of the Form-VI notice, it was complied with yet failure to mention the same in the offence report, casts a shadow of doubt on the genuineness of Ext.1.

On the other hand, incross-examination, the PW1/Food Inspector has categorically deposed that the samples, which he had purchased, was even not packed and materials for packing the same were by the side of the bread, he purchased, meaning thereby that it was not ready for sale.
Such evidence of the PW1/complainant and the contents of the Form-VI notice are found to be inconsistent.
15. During cross
-examination of PW1

, he also deposed that about 50 breads were under Page No.#
4/5 process of packing.
If such is the evidence of PW1, there is no clear evidence to that effect that he had purchased the packaged bread only.
On the other hand, in Form-VI notice, it is stated that he had taken the sample of the bread stored for sale.
If his such statement, in the form-VI notice, is correct, then it could not have been processed for packaging; rather, packaging was complete and then only stored for sale.
Therefore, such evidence of PW1, Food Inspector, is not found to be consistent; therefore, not reliable.

16. So far as taking of sample in presence of independent witness is concerned, as required under Section 10(7) of the PFA Act, the Food Inspector shall call one or more persons to be present at the time of taking the sample and also obtain their signatures, under Section 10(3) of the said Act.
17.

In the instant case, the evidence of PW1, the Food Inspector, makes it appear that while he intended to take sample of the bread, he went out of the bakery and requested three independent persons to sign, but they did not oblige him.

Thereafter, he came to the bakery and requested 2/3 customers, who also did not oblige him, such evidence did not appear to have been corroborated by the evidence of PW2, the office Peon of the Food Inspector, who accompanied him and was all along with him.
Calling of independent witnesses being a question of fact needs to be proved by corroborative evidence.
But, it has not been proved as PW2 is silent on this aspect.
18. Apart from all these facts, the fact to the effect that the bread, sample of which was taken, was not packed at the relevant point of time; rather, were under way of packing.
Therefore, naturally and logically the date of manufacturing etc. would not have been there.

Crl.Rev.P./383/2009 on 28 January, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3387268/
3 19.

The Public Analysts report, exhibited, vide Ext.14, speaks of violation of Rule 38(f) of the PFA Rules and there is no opinion therein that the sample, so collected by the PW1, was unfit for human consumption.

20. Considering such evidence on record, on hearing the respective learned counsel for the parties,
as indicated above, this Court is of the view that the prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the accused-revision petitioner for an offence under Section 7 of the PFA Act, punishable under Section 16 thereof.

Therefore, the judgment of the learned trial Court as well as the learned appellate Court do not appear to have based on evidence on record; rather, the Page No.# 5/5 same is palpably against the evidence on record.

21. This Court is aware of the fact that in a revision petition, we cannot re-appreciate the evidence,
but the law on this point has been settled by now to the effect that if there is apparent, glaring inconsistency in appreciation of the evidence on record, the same can be interfered with by the High Court in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction.

Therefore, the findings of the learned trial Court,
convicting and sentencing the accused-revision petitioner, is set aside being not consistent with the evidence.
Therefore, the accused-revision petitioner stands acquitted.
22. Accordingly, the revision petition is allowed.

23. Send down the LCR along with a copy of this judgment and order.
JUDGE
